claims.text: A supervised machine-learning model combining DFT-derived vibrational density-of-states features, atomic mass variance, and bond-length disorder descriptors will predict lattice thermal conductivity more accurately than mass-variance-only empirical models.
The proposed approach applies to equimolar, single-phase FCC or BCC HEAs containing 4–6 transition-metal elements.
The target alloys have random elemental distributions and minimal second-phase precipitates.
The model uses small-cell DFT phonon density-of-states signatures as predictive descriptors.
The model also uses atomic mass variance and local bond-length disorder descriptors.
Predictions are scoped to bulk polycrystalline samples at 300 K with average grain size greater than 1 μm and porosity below 1%.
Vibrational fingerprints and bond-length disorder metrics capture dominant phonon-scattering mechanisms caused by atomic-scale disorder.
Representing these disorder-related scattering mechanisms will reduce the systematic bias of mass-variance-only approaches.
The proposed model will reduce mean absolute error in lattice-thermal-conductivity predictions by 20–30% relative to the baseline.
The proposed model will correctly rank low-thermal-conductivity candidates in the top decile in at least 80% of cases.
Mass-variance-only empirical models yield approximately 40% mean absolute error for equimolar 4–6-element HEAs.
The model may not generalize to non-equimolar alloys, alloys with more than six elements, multiphase microstructures, or highly anharmonic systems.
Limited training data in HEA composition space produces approximately ±10% uncertainty in the estimated error reduction.
A blind validation set of ten equimolar, 4–6-element, single-phase HEAs can be used to compare the proposed and baseline models.
Room-temperature lattice thermal conductivity for the validation alloys will be measured using TDTR.
The hypothesis is falsified if the proposed model fails to achieve at least a 10% lower mean absolute error than the baseline across the validation set.

contradictions.description: The central prediction requires a 20–30% error reduction, but the model is falsified only below a 10% reduction. An observed 10–19% reduction would contradict the quantified prediction without satisfying the stated falsification rule.
The hypothesis predicts at least 80% success in top-decile ranking, but the benchmark and falsification rule evaluate only mean absolute error and provide no decisive test of the ranking claim.
